covering.note: Its skin is smooth, with just a few small bumps.

size.note: It is only 2.5 to 3.5 cm long.

activity.note: It often sits in patches of sunlight.

social.note: It lives in small colonies in certain patches of forest.

trees.note: It hides among fallen leaves on the ground.

young.note: A female lays about 40 eggs, though fewer in the far south.

lifespan.note: Some are still breeding at 15 years old.

clues.text: Its snout ends in a soft, pointy tip.
It can be brown or bright green, matching the ground where it sits.
Its belly is black with big white spots.
It lives in the fallen leaves of southern beech forests.
The father carries the tadpoles inside his throat pouch until they turn into froglets.
Main threats: forests cut down or replaced with pine plantations, and chytrid, a fungus that kills frogs.
Zoos in Chile and Germany breed it as a backup population.
When threatened, it rolls onto its back and plays dead.
It sits still and waits for insects to come close.

facts.text: Charles Darwin found this frog in Chile during his voyage on HMS Beagle.
The tadpoles live in their father's throat pouch for about 6 weeks, then hop out as tiny frogs.
Its whole home can be just 1 to 3 square meters: about the size of a bath mat.
The father feeds the tadpoles in his pouch with a thick liquid he makes.
When they are done changing, the froglets come out through their father's mouth.
In the cold months it shelters under logs and moss.
A scared frog near a stream may jump in and float on its back.
Females lay their eggs in the leaf litter on the forest floor.
As many as 19 young have been found in one father's pouch.
It has vanished from many places where it was common until the 1980s.
